title: Medications and Root Canals: What to Tell Your Dentist
metaTitle: Medications & Root Canals: What to Tell Your Dentist
metaDescription: Which medications matter before a root canal? Why your full health history, blood thinners, allergies, and the truth about antibiotics are all worth sharing.
excerpt: Your medications and medical history shape how a root canal is planned. Here is what to share, why blood thinners and allergies matter, and why antibiotics are not a cure.
heroImageAlt: A patient reviewing a medication list with a dentist before treatment.
bodyHtml:
Why your medications matter before a root canal

Before a root canal, one of the most helpful things you can do is give your dentist a complete picture of your health: every medication you take (including over-the-counter products and supplements), any allergies, and any medical conditions. This information shapes how your treatment is planned and helps keep it safe. A common question is whether you will need antibiotics first — and the key point is that antibiotics are not a substitute for treating the tooth. They may play a role in certain situations, but the decision belongs to your dentist based on your specific case, not to a general rule.

What to tell your dentist

Aim to share the following, ideally written down so nothing is forgotten:

  • All medications and supplements. Prescription drugs, over-the-counter pain relievers, vitamins, and herbal supplements can all be relevant. Bring the names and doses if you can.
  • Blood thinners and anticoagulants. If you take medication that affects bleeding or clotting, your dentist needs to know. Do not stop any such medication on your own — always check with the professional who prescribed it first.
  • Allergies. Mention any allergies or past reactions, including to medications, latex, or local anaesthetic, so safe alternatives can be chosen.
  • Medical conditions. Heart conditions, diabetes, immune-related conditions, pregnancy, and other health issues can influence planning. Some specific heart conditions, for example, prompt a discussion about preventive antibiotics, but this is individualised.
  • Recent changes. New diagnoses, recent surgeries, or medications you have just started or stopped are all worth flagging.

The truth about antibiotics

It is a common misconception that antibiotics can clear up a tooth that needs a root canal. In reality, a true infection inside a tooth generally cannot be resolved by antibiotics alone, because the source of the problem is inside the tooth where medication cannot reliably reach it. Antibiotics are sometimes used as a supporting measure in particular circumstances — for example when infection has spread — but they do not replace the need to treat or remove the affected tissue. Taking antibiotics may temporarily ease symptoms while leaving the underlying problem unaddressed, which is why timely dental care still matters. Using antibiotics only when genuinely needed also supports responsible use and reduces the risk of resistance.

Do I need antibiotics before a root canal?

Not routinely. For most people, a root canal does not require antibiotics beforehand. Whether they are appropriate depends on factors such as the presence and spread of infection and certain medical conditions. Your dentist will decide based on your situation — this is not something to self-prescribe or assume.

Why does my dentist need to know about supplements and herbal products?

Some vitamins, herbal products, and supplements can affect bleeding, interact with other medications, or be relevant to healing, even though they are available without a prescription. Because they are easy to overlook, it is worth listing them alongside your prescription medications so your dentist has the complete picture and nothing important is missed.

Should I keep taking my regular medications?

In general, yes — continue your prescribed medications unless your dentist or the prescribing professional specifically tells you otherwise. Stopping medication on your own, including blood thinners, can carry its own risks. If a change is ever needed, it should be coordinated with the right professional.

What if I take over-the-counter painkillers for the toothache?

That is common and usually fine, but still mention it, along with how much and how often, so your dentist has the full picture. They can also advise on what pain relief is suitable before and after treatment.

A shared, informed plan

Being open about your health history lets your dental team tailor your care safely — there is no such thing as too much relevant information. If you want to discuss your medications or medical history before treatment, you can get in touch with Smile Dental Arts Centre in Markham through the clinic's contact page. Dr. Neda Kadivar is a general and family dentist with over 20 years of experience and a member of the Royal College of Dental Surgeons of Ontario.

This article is general information and not a substitute for professional dental advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always speak with a licensed dentist about your specific situation.
